# Preserved Lemons

## Ingredients

- 6 unwaxed lemons, plus 2 more for their juice
- 5% salt by weight of the fruit, weighed precisely
- 1 bay leaf
- a few black peppercorns
- a small glass weight or a clean scrunched jar lid to hold the fruit down

## Method

I weigh the lemons first, because the salt is 5% of their weight and nothing else, so six lemons at roughly 1 kg means 50 g of salt and no guessing. I scrub the fruit under warm water to lift any wax, dry them, and trim the little stalk ends. Then I quarter each lemon lengthwise almost to the base, stopping about a centimetre short so the four segments stay joined at the bottom and the fruit opens like a flower.

I rub the salt into the cut faces and into the opened fruit, working it into every fold, then pack the lemons into a clean jar one at a time, pressing each down hard with the back of a spoon so they release their own juice. I tuck the bay leaf and the peppercorns down the side of the jar, and I keep pressing until the lemons are tightly packed and the brine they have given up covers them completely. If the juice does not quite cover the top, I squeeze in extra lemons until it does, because the fruit must stay submerged through the whole cure.

I slide the glass weight in on top and seal the jar. I leave it in a cool cupboard, not the fridge, and turn it gently every few days to move the brine around. After about four weeks the rind has gone soft and translucent and the brine smells deeply sour and salty. I keep the jar in the cupboard for as long as it lasts, always making sure the lemons stay under the liquid, and I rinse each piece under cold water before use because the flesh and the brine are far too salty to eat straight from the jar. Once the jar is open I keep it in the fridge to slow the cure down, and it lasts for well over a year.

## Notes

The 5% salt figure is the one number worth getting right, because too little and the lemons spoil before they cure, and too much and the rind never softens. Working by weight rather than by spoonfuls makes the result repeatable from one batch to the next. The lemons have to be unwaxed, since the wax seals the skin and stops the salt soaking into the rind. Pressing the fruit down hard enough to collapse it is what frees the juice that becomes the brine, and that is the part that takes some confidence the first time. A cool cupboard is better than a fridge here because the cure moves faster and the fruit develops a deeper flavour, though a fridge works if your kitchen runs warm. The most common failure is fruit that floats above the liquid, which goes soft and mouldy, so the weight is not optional. Rinse the quarters before use and scrape out the pulp, then chop the rind fine for tagines, salads and dressings. It keeps for a year or more if the brine stays over it. The rind is the part worth using, chopped fine and stirred into a tagine or a dressing, and the pulp can go into a marinade where its salt is welcome. Lemon varieties with thin skins cure fastest, and a couple of extra lemons on hand for juice saves a trip to the shop if the first pressing runs short.
